review:
Cooperative role-playing game in which two players escape from prison together and experience a cinematic story full of action and excitement

ATTENTION! ONLY BUY IF YOU HAVE A FRIEND, THIS IS NOT A SOLO GAME!

✅Well-designed screen split between players
✅Good graphics made with Unreal Engine 4
✅Co-op gameplay without the need to buy two copies of the game (One person just needs to buy it and the other can play via Remote Play Together)
✅Lots of mini-games during the story (bench press, dips, darts, basketball, baseball, etc.). For me, the best mini-game is keeping your balance in a wheelchair XD
✅Very diverse characters. Vincent is a calm person who prefers to negotiate, while Leo is an impulsive person who prefers forceful solutions
✅During the game, there will be several moments where you will have to decide whether to choose Leo's or Vincent's approach, but this has no impact on the final storyline 
✅In the game, you can interact with a huge number of characters. Even with the same person, two players can approach them and the dialogue will be slightly different. There are also mini-tasks that you don't have to complete, such as repairing a motorbike
✅Very good soundtrack that perfectly emphasises the atmosphere of each scene, from moments where the characters have to talk quietly to very dynamic races where a lot is happening
✅The game offers us great variety. We have QTE sequences, escaping from prison and from the police, searching houses, driving a car and shooting. Everything is here. 
✅Wide variety of locations, from a dark prison we have to escape from to beautiful nature where we light a fire and sit with a friend, and later through a dark forest in Mexico 
✅Very engaging storyline of our two heroes, Vincent and Leo, who do not trust each other at first, but after a few shared ideas and escaping from prison, they begin to trust each other and would stand up for each other 
✅The ending is very interesting and surprising for us
✅The price is okay if two people buy it, because the game shouldn't cost £30 for 6 hours of gameplay (I have over 10 because I played with two people)

✅❌ The game is very linear, so I don't know whether to consider this an advantage or a disadvantage; each player must decide for themselves (I like games that focus heavily on the storyline

❌Poor shooting system, imprecise shooting (I played on a gamepad and found this to be the case, as did my friend who played on a keyboard) 
❌The AL of the opponents during shooting also turned out to be very poor, because the opponent was standing literally 3 metres away from me and was shooting at my ally who was standing much further away 
❌Another point I will mention about shooting is why I can't shoot at a dead person :D
❌In the game, you can't see our characters running at all
❌I don't know if it was supposed to be like that, but I didn't like the fact that when we were at the airport, we could hear ‘airplanes approaching’ in the background, but in reality, no planes arrived

[b]If you’ve ever wanted to know exactly how much you trust your best friend, or how quickly you’d sell them out for a cinematic escape, A Way Out is the game that will give you the answer. Developed by Hazelight Studios and led by the ever-energetic Josef Fares, this isn’t just a game you play, it’s an experience you share.
Here is why this prison-break-turned-road-trip is one of the most unique titles in the last decade, and why you absolutely need a "Player 2" to survive it.[/b]

[h1]Two Men, One Screen, No Solitude[/h1]
[b]The first thing you need to know is that A Way Out cannot be played alone. There is no AI partner. There is no "single-player mode." You are either sitting on a couch with a buddy or playing online with a friend.
The game uses a constant split-screen perspective, even when you're playing online. At first, it’s a bit jarring to see your friend’s perspective taking up half your monitor, but then the genius of it sinks in. While you’re busy distracting a guard in the laundry room, you can literally watch your partner sneak through the vents on their half of the screen. It creates a level of synchronized storytelling that most games can’t touch. It turns "I'm doing this" into "We are doing this," and that's a rare feeling in modern gaming.[/b]

[h1]The Odd Duo: Leo and Vincent[/h1]
[b]The story follows Leo, a hot-headed, punch-first-ask-questions-later kind of guy, and Vincent, the more calculated, stoic newcomer. You and your partner choose one, and you’re stuck with them for the ride.
What starts as a standard Shawshank Redemption prison break quickly spirals into a high-stakes revenge thriller across the 1970s. The writing isn't Shakespeare, it’s more like a gritty, B-movie action flick, but that’s exactly where the charm lies. You’ll go from intense stealth sequences to high-speed boat chases, and then, inexplicably, spend twenty minutes playing Connect Four or arm-wrestling your friend in a trailer park.
The pacing is frantic, moving from one "Wait, we’re doing this now?" moment to the next. It keeps you on your toes, and honestly, the sheer variety of activities prevents the game from ever feeling stale.[/b]

[h1]The "Friend Pass" and the Technical Side[/h1]
[b]A massive shout-out to the developers for the "Friend Pass." Only one person needs to own the game for two people to play the entire thing together online. In an era of microtransactions and "pay-to-win," this feels like a genuine gift to the players. Visually, the game holds up well. It’s not trying to be the most graphically advanced title on Steam, but the art direction, the lighting in the 70s-style environments, and the cinematic camera work (which often merges the two screens into one beautiful shot) make it feel like a high-budget movie.[/b]


[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]The Emotional Gut-Punch: Without spoiling anything, the ending will leave you and your friend staring at the credits in silence. It’s a bold narrative choice that pays off.
[*]Pure Variety: You’re never doing one thing for too long. One minute it’s a stealth mission, the next it’s a 2D-style side-scroller fight, the next it’s a rhythm-based banjo duet.
[*]The Price Point: With the Friend Pass, the value for money is unbeatable.
[*]The Minigames: Honestly, I spent more time trying to beat my friend at horseshoes than I did actually escaping the police.
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Mandatory Co-op: If your friends are busy or you’re a lone wolf, you literally cannot play this game.
[*]A Bit Janky: The shooting mechanics and some of the movement can feel a little stiff compared to AAA titles.
[*]One-and-Done: Once you know the twists and turns, there’s not a huge reason to replay it, other than switching characters to see the slightly different dialogue.
[/list]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
[b]Look, A Way Out is a rare breed. It’s a game that respects your time (it’s about 6-8 hours long) and prioritizes the social experience over everything else. It’s funny, it’s tense, it’s occasionally a bit cheesy, and by the end, it’s genuinely moving.
If you have a friend you trust (or one you want to test), grab a copy, grab some snacks, and prepare for a weekend you won’t forget. Just try not to stay mad at them when they inevitably mess up a stealth section and get you both caught for the fifth time. A cinematic triumph for the "Buddy Cop" genre.[/b]

I've played A Way Out twice now, with a few years and It Takes Two and Split Fiction in between. It's clear that Josef Fares has grown a lot as a writer. A Way Out isn't a bad story by any means, but it's definitely less polished than the co-op masterpieces that came after. Still, you can tell this game laid the groundwork for the cinematic, emotional split-screen experiences Hazelight would later perfect.

The co-op gameplay is fun and varied—except for that damn boat ride, which tested our patience more than our coordination. While the story can be tropey and a bit cheesy at times, it’s still engaging and well-paced. I appreciated that it kept us moving through new scenarios without dragging.

I really liked both Vincent and Leo. Leo, in particular, has a surprisingly healthy relationship with his partner, which was refreshing to see in a crime drama like this.

One major drawback for me is the ending. Without spoiling anything, it felt a bit too forced. The player has little to no agency in how things unfold, which took away some of the emotional payoff for me.

Also, needing to go through the EA launcher is a huge con. It’s clunky and unnecessary.

That said, I’d still recommend A Way Out to:

- People who’ve never tried a split-screen co-op narrative game

- Fans of Split Fiction or It Takes Two who are okay with something a little rougher around the edges

It's not perfect, but it’s an important step in a fantastic evolution of co-op storytelling.

A way out is a very innovative multiplayer cooperative game. Before this game, I never thought that a multi-player cooperative game could have such gameplay - as the predecessor and exploration of the It takes two, this one no doubt showed us the possibility of the split screen game.

The gameplay of the game is not very innovative, but these gameplays combined with split-screen play can bring players a unique gaming experience. The plot of the game is unexpected and exciting, and I'm not too impressed with the music. The game's picture and graphics quality and rendering level are very good, and you can enjoy a visual feast.

Finally, this game is not very suitable for playing with strangers, I think playing with friends is the only way to get the complete game experience. Another shortcoming of the game is that the game duration is relatively short, but this game will not let you down. At the same time, as the developer's first attempt to split-screen games, there are many places in the game that more or less make players feel that this is an experimental game, and perhaps players also need to be tolerant.

If I were to list any downside to the game, it would be it's unskippable cutscenes (even after you've finished the game multiple times), a lack of ability to injure/kill friendlies (not counting letting enemies kill your friend) and perhaps a bit too much in the way of locked combat/animation. Me and my friend had fun with this one, but this is not a masterpiece thats for sure. It was a beautiful aspiration: to make a co-op game that encourages people to work together by means of original gameplay. But in the end, the manner in which A Way Out is played is seldom original and it's written like a poor action movie out of the 90's.

5/10 - worth playing and have fun with a friend, but, buy it as cheap as you can.

Vincent get's taken hostage by Leo, they drive off a bridge, then Vincent gets in a Helicopter as Leo boats away. What would you do at this point? Likewise, when the boat DOES explode (you can decide to not shoot it, it will explode of it's own volition) you both take up two sides of a building to shoot each other. [h1]Introduction[/h1]
[b]A Way Out[/b] is a heavily story-driven action-adventure game that tells the story of two convicts, [i]Leo[/i] and [i]Vincent[/i]. The catch is that the game is playable only in co-op. The game supports both local and online options, and you can use [b]Steam Remote Play[/b] to stream it to your friend, or you can use [b]Friend Pass[/b] on [b]Origin[/b], where your friend just needs to download the game files, and you will invite him to your lobby. You can also play with random people online, but you cannot play it alone.
[h3]Story[/h3]
The whole game feels like a good action film with several interesting plot twists. The story itself starts in a prison where both [i]Leo[/i] and [i]Vincent[/i] ended up because of a guy called [i]Harvey[/i]. As their path crossed during a few incidents, they decided to work together, escape the prison, and find [i]Harvey[/i]. Both characters are unique in their own way as [i]Leo[/i] is more of a guy who first acts rather than thinks, and [i]Vincent[/i] is the exact opposite of him, which leads to several humorous and a bit unpredictable situations. I would say that their personality is interesting and likable, as I was interested in their problems and related side characters, like family members. 

On the opposite, the villain [i]Harvey[/i] is just an uninteresting figure who does not have any depth at all, and the game would prosper from fleshing out his character more. There are also a few situations that do not make sense, and they break my immersion a bit. For example, if a character has another person as a human shield, its weapon’s ammo is unlimited, and he does not reload it at all. However, even with all these problems, I enjoyed the story, as [i]Vincent’s[/i] and [i]Leo’s[/i] journey was thrilling and emotional. In the end, I will remember some story twists for a while.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2152142398
[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
I highly recommend playing this game with your partner, friend, or another relative, as it adds a lot to the experience rather than with random people. The game lasts about [b]six hours[/b], and I would say that the length is just right. I could probably argue that one more hour could help flesh out some characters, but it would still be quite short. Most of the time, you have to go through small open locations and finish the task to continue to another section. One of the most used gameplay mechanics are quick-timed events, which are surprisingly done right, and there is no tremendous button mashing, so that is a plus. However, do not expect some complex gameplay or mechanics. This game relies on quick-timed events and short different elements. The gameplay is tailored to fit the story, you will not find here difficult puzzles as in [b]Portal[/b] series or more complex combat options as in [b]Borderlands[/b] series. The game is very forgiving, and the checkpoints are very common.

Throughout the chapters, the game changes the environment, tasks, and gameplay activities a lot. The co-operation of both players is very important as you cannot finish the game without it. There are a lot of easy environmental puzzles that fit the narrative and linearity of the game, but I would still wish for at least a few more complex tasks. Sometimes the game lets you deal out with enemies via stealth or shooting. Unfortunately, AI is quite stupid, so you can rush through the area quickly and knock them out. As for shooting, the gunplay is quite good but a bit easy, as well. However, sections, where you drive vehicles, are a bit harder as you mostly fight the camera (this, especially, applies to the bikes). I would welcome some difficulty settings, at least for the enemies. If you are looking for a challenging co-op experience, then you will not find it here.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2152148836
The game also offers various activities and minigames, which are only present in specific chapters. For example, you can throw darts, play videogames, interact with others, and much more. I am not going to name them all, but it varies a lot throughout the chapters, and it keeps the game fresh and interesting. Even if you decide not to do them, you will still receive a fair amount of diverse gameplay.

Sometimes the game offers you a choice to continue in certain situations differently. It changes cutscenes and gameplay a bit, so small replay value for at least one more playthrough is here. To put a clear picture, you might decide if you will try to cross the bridge with the police in a car, which is the fastest but more dangerous variant, or if you will go underneath the bridge. Speaking about choices, the game also has two endings, but none of the previous choices matters, as they are more about how do you continue your journey gameplay-wise rather than about longtime story effect. The thing I disliked about this mechanic is that both players have to actually choose the same option. If two players will not choose the same thing then you wait until one of you decides to side with the other player. The game should have implemented an RNG system that would choose in such situations.

The second thing I did not like much about the gameplay is how the screen is split in half even in online co-op. I understand this is necessary for local co-op, but it is a bit irritating as your screen is smaller for the whole game. There were few occasions where the game actually let play only one player and the scenes transmitted rather than being cut in half. This option was way more enjoyable and film-like. It would probably also add a bit to the difficulty, as you would not have an option to look to your partner's side.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2152151105
[h3]Audiovisuals & Performance[/h3]
The game looks great graphics-wise. It offers several beautiful sceneries and cutscenes which might be comparable to films. There are several animations for different situations, and they are properly fleshed out. The only minor issue is that you can drive through a few branches during car chases which destroys an immersion a bit, and I would not expect this in this linear short game. As for the sounds, the sound effects themselves are of high quality. As for the soundtrack, there are few compelling compositions, but nothing memorable. 

The game was tested with an [b]i5 8300H, GTX 1060 6GB, and 16GB RAM[/b], running at high settings at [b]60[/b] frames per second, at [b]1920x1080[/b] resolution. The game ran without any problems and crashes. However, the connection with [b]Origin[/b] servers caused troubles a few times, as sometimes my partner got kicked, and I could not invite her again, as [b]Origin[/b] did not show her in online status. For a short game like this, it is pretty annoying but, fortunately, the game has many save spots, so you can jump right back to where you ended.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Even with the aforementioned shortcomings, I can still easily recommend this game, especially if it is on sale. It is an enjoyable, thrilling, and captivating story-driven experience, and I wish there would be more games like this.

The best split-screen co-op game so far

Before you consider buying this game, make sure that you have a friend or family member that is willing to play hours of this game with you, because this is a co-op only game.

A Way Out is a one of a kind game. Usually, massive story-driven games are only for single player and it's hard to share the kind of experience that these types of games give you. A Way Out, however, allows you to experience a massive story-driven game with a friend. Playing the two characters gives completely different perspectives on the story. The two characters often get separated and do unique things while still kind of connected. Playing a different character after finishing the game gives a completely different version of the game.

All the levels are creative and use split-screen co-op's advantages to its best. The cinematic camera angles and changes of screen placements are pleasant and well designed. In the hospital level where the players take turns to controls their characters in full screen, the use of cinematic transitions and long camera shots are amazing. The different choices that the players can vote on could have some influence on how the game plays. These choices don't change anything major, but they make some parts of the levels different.

The story of A Way Out is great and the endings are unexpected and emotional. The characters are pretty well made, and their emotions seem real. There are many mini-games scattered around the story for the players to compete with each other. Some of them are not well made, but it's always fun to mess around with a friend and have a little fun.

At some later parts of the game, the characters get guns and start shooting people. The aiming is a bit weird, especially if you are playing with a controller. Those parts just feel like a cheaper and more boring version of Uncharted 4 without all the grappling hooks and moving around the environment.

There is barely any game out there that targets split-screen co-op as a major selling point except for A Way Out. I highly recommend trying it out with a friend or family member. I hope there are more good co-op story-driven games like this in the future.

The Pros First!

[h1] Review [/h1]

It is no surprise to see Josef Fares deliver a AAA title for the indie scene. A Way Out plays like a blockbuster mastodon but with the subtleness and creativity of sophomore cinephiles. It surprises, it captivates and it goes all the way in every single possible way. This is how Spielberg would have directed a video game and this is how your summer matinee guilty pleasure would have been brought to life in an interactive experience, all the while leaving very little to scrutinize and hark down upon. A Way Out is a love letter to cinema and a flirtatious invite for us monkey brains to be able to adventure in the shoes of our big screen hero. A POV dream come true.

That is basically the gist of the success I address this game, as it more often than not plays itself with easy mechanics and button holding skill checks. It is an immersive marvel that elevates a movie script into being larger than life through the eyes and fingers of the players. The game comes alive, much to the credit of its tight writing and editing. Camera shots that would impress you normally is elevated even further in the context of you playing the scene out. A Way Out is absolute cinema on the PC, but what about the game?

It plays out as a co-op split screen where you pilot a supposed main character each. You more often than not are assigned your own goal and free roam with npc chatting and minigames at your disposal, while coming together now and then for high stake quick time events or chases. The gameplay ranges from stealth, vehicle riding and gunplay, with adventure game feel in between. It is all pleasantly amusing and carefully balanced in the narrative, with slower moments surprising you with effectual progressions. You simply do not want it to end. The good thing is that you can take your time with before-mentioned dialogues and carefully sprinkled minigames. Maybe you just want to compete in Connect Four, pitch some ball or play some music together while gallivanting through the scenarios. A Way Out is not a gameplay masterclass but it can truly entertain you and give that well needed escape from reality.

The story is at points hammy but goes through enough change in scenery and objective that you wholeheartedly keep being excited for what lies beyond the next story beat. The unlikely pair of protagonists in the abrasive Leo and methodical Vincent keeps an equilibrium of humor and heart; while you escape prison and set out to right the wrongdoings that has befallen you.

Some passing negatives on my [i]way out[/i] would be that the acting is not always up to snuff even though Josef's brother Fares Fares (that is his name) puts in a stellar showing as Leo. Graphics look great but will not age particularly well and the whole easy co-op spiel will definitely be a turn off for some. In a way it was for my duo who found it at times uneventful and void of gameplay, but did in the end still enjoy the time we put into it. That is after all the biggest crux of A Way Out. If you do not have someone that shares your interests, a playthrough might result in a monumental waste of time and money, as you are supposed to relish in it together. I am for one happy I had the privilege to do so.

The story is quite good, it comes from the developers of Brothers a Tale of Two Sons. There are two characters – Vincent and Leo. They meet in the prison and decide to break out of it for revenge.
From the very beginning you need to learn to work together to bypass various situations and threats. While the game is mainly story driven I wouldn't call it a fully narrative experience. There's quite some gameplay there and it's pretty diverse. Mostly you'll be walking around or sneaking while figuring out how to get to where you need. Which isn't hard by the way, there are no real puzzles. But it has other gameplay mechanics like rowing the boat, driving and shooting. While all of these usually are very poorly executed in similar games, here they work well. Of course don't expect super deep driving physics or shooting mechanics but driving feels smooth, sometimes it feels like a proper racing game. And shooting is also decently done and isn't clunky at all, mostly it works as cover based shooter.
Gameplay changes often and there's always something new so the game doesn't become boring or repetitive.

You do stuff by pressing or tapping buttons, sometimes in perfect sync with another character, there are no moments when another character has nothing to do. There are sections when one character is more busy than the other but at these moments you still can explore the surroundings, speak with people or play some mini-games. There are mini-games for both players too. Oh and i encourage you to speak with people since that leads to some funny dialogues and little stories. On top of that there are easter eggs which are tied to achievements and roughly half of them are really fun to do because they lead to some short cut-scenes, mostly funny ones.
In general gameplay is nearly perfect and has perfect amount of everything, calm moments of silence, talking, action, running and so on. It feels like a really long movie.

Graphically the game looks good. Surroundings are beautifully crafted with lots of small details around and things to interact with while character models are good but could be better, it's nowhere near Man of Medan or Quantic Dream games. Although facial animations and expressions are quite good.

Performance is perfect, game runs on max settings at 90-100fps easily, played on 5800x, 2070s, 32gb @3440x1440. There's ultrawide support but it's weird. Sometimes when there's a scene of only one character the image is in correct aspect ratio but smaller with black space around it. But there are some moments when the screen space is fully utilized so ultrawide works.

Voice acting and sound are good too. Music feels like it's from a movie and plays along nicely with the mood of the scenes. Voice acting sometimes could be ok only but mostly it is good.

Overall a very good coop story driven game with diverse gameplay, cool movie-like action scenes and dramatic moments. Definitely worth a buy. Not at full price though since the game is short and has no replayability value. Achievement hunting and another ending could net you an additional hour or so since it has chapter select but that's it.

[u][b]Lifespan :[/b][/u] ~7 hours to finish the story while taking your time and messing around a little.

[u][b]Story :[/b][/u] You are two inmates, one who just got incarcerated and another one who has been there for 6 months already. You quickly realise that you both ended up in prison because of a crime boss named Harvey and you decide to escape prison to take revenge on him.
The prison is actually just a small part of the game, your adventure will go much farther than those walls! The characters will get to learn about each other and decide on what to do to reach their goal. The story is kinda typical but there are some twists that we personally didn't expect at all. In any case it was very enjoyable and we were completely immersed in it (you feel it when you or your partner is in danger!).

[u][b]Gameplay :[/b][/u] The screen is split in two so you can both see what the other is doing and when something important is happening to one character then his screen will extend and cover the other one for a bit. The same thing will happen if there is a shared cutscene, but this time making the two screens fuse. This feels a little weird at the beginning, but you quickly get used to it and it's really nice to see what the other is up to, especially when you split up.
The story is divided into scenes/chapters. You go to a place, you do this, then you move on to another scene. You can usually mess around in the scenes and they are big enough to not feel trapped. But it does feel sometimes that you are jumping from one to another a bit hastily.
The two characters have very different personalities and will not react the same way to things or dialogues. One is reckless while the other is more cautious. Sometimes when choosing a way to pass an obstacle you'll have to choose which character's plan to follow. But it's also in the little things: when prompted a character will break the locked window while the other will try to find another way. The choices, even the little ones, really help with the immersion.
There are several puzzles (ex: how to get this thing out of this room without the guards noticing). From what I have seen, there are always several ways to reach your goal.
There are some action scenes too, where you need for example to run away from things. Again, we were really into it and trying hard to succeed. If you fail though (which happens rarely because the emphasis is clearly put on the story/adventure and not on the challenge), you will be brought back to a nearby checkpoint.
There are lots of little things scattered through the levels to have fun with your partner. There are often silly things: cut the wood because... why not? Play a board game or darts with your partner and get the highest score. And as silly and useless as it sounds, we would always seek them out to try them, because they were actually fun.

[u][b]Achievements :[/b][/u] Little hidden things throughout the levels; like tell this to that person, play that game, get this score, do this silly thing... Nothing annoying. You can replay a specific level so it was really easy to go back and get them all after our playthrough.
